newsitem.title: UK: London precious metals turn generally easier.
newsitem.headline: London precious metals turn generally easier.

text.p: Precious metals prices eased from morning levels on Thursday afternoon as New York adjusted to lower levels established in Europe.
Dealers noted the dollar was off its closing low against the yen, which reduced some of the incentive to trade gold. The yen's strength had been supporting gold recently.
Bullion fixed 20 cents lower than the morning at $342.75 per ounce and against a previous close of $342.40/$342.90, while the Comex June contract was down $0.40 at $343.60.
Most of the weakness came from the platinum group metals and especially palladium, which was sold by Swiss dealers early in Europe and fell steeply on the Nymex opening.
Palladium has lost steadily since it peaked at its second highest fix on record of $180.50 on Wednesday morning.
News that Russia plans to begin shipping its delayed 1997 exports shortly and that volume will match 1996 levels has taken some of the verve out of the market.
However, dealers were far from certain palladium's rally was over.
"According to what we have heard, the Tiger fund has the market were it wants it," one dealer said referring to the much publicised buying by Tiger Management earlier this year.

Some other dealers forecast the funds hanging on to palladium positions until the price was "up to $300", according to one, and others forecast a biting squeeze on Nymex once the June contract went into its notice period next week.
Open interest was over 5,000 lots on the contract on May 20 but this was dismissed as being too obvious a play by some dealers here.
Platinum was also easier at $387.75/$388.75, down $5.75 from the close but still commanding a premium of over $55 to gold.
Like its sister metal, platinum was well sold early in Europe and came under pressure again when New York opened.
Gold business was unexceptional and reflected a slightly stronger dollar following a rise in jobless figures to 322,000 from the revised 319,000 the previous week.
Silver was quiet but, like the rest of the complex, was expected to drift lower as the long holiday weekend in London approached.
It was quoted at $4.67/$4.69, down two cents from Wednesday's close.
